# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# A Critical Reading of the Varga & Holm Comment on the Halden Pilot

Most of this comment is good forensic work. Sections 1–5 confirm and quantify the main weaknesses in the Halden paper, several of which I flagged earlier. The problem is the conclusion: the claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the comment's own corrected estimate and by the Varden trial it cites selectively.

## Arithmetic checks

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Table 2 rows | 98.7/0.8; 95.1/0.8; 98.4/0.859; 95.4/0.861 | +23.4%, +18.9%, +14.6%, +10.8% ✓ |
| Hours fall (27 organisations) | 34.6/40.3 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Hours fall (17 organisations) | 34.8/40.4 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014/1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |
| Hours components | 32 + (0.7 × 4) + 1.6 | **36.4 hours, not 34.6** ✗ |
| Novelty extrapolation | 0.29 ÷ (0.32/3 per month) ≈ 2.7 months after month 6 | **about month 9, not "around month ten"** (minor) |

The hours inconsistency needs explaining. The two sources the authors cite, longer days and work on the day off, add up to about 36.4 hours a week. That is nearly 2 hours more than the 34.6 they report. Either the components are averaged over different sets of organisations, or one of the figures is wrong. The 34.6 figure is the more favourable one for reduced hours, so the error doesn't obviously favour the authors' case. But it is the denominator of their main correction, so it should be resolved.

## What the comment establishes

1. **The Halden paper misdescribed its attrition.** Seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule began, and six cited workload or output. "Withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons" is not an accurate summary. This is the most serious finding against the original paper.
2. **Manager ratings ran high.** In 19 of 23 organisations, the manager's index was above the record-based index. A sign test makes that very unlikely to be chance (p ≈ 0.003). The 23 organisations' manager-reported mean (98.9) is close to the full sample's (98.7), which suggests the subset is not unusual on that measure.
3. **Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.** This matches Varden's 13% for case-processing closely.
4. **Real revenue fell.** The 1.4% nominal rise is a fall of about 2.6% once inflation is removed.
5. **The "sector-general" claim was an artifact of the metric.** Any output index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain when hours fall 20%.

## Problems with the comment

### 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own evidence

The authors' best corrected estimate is a **+10.8%** gain in output per actual hour. They then call the gains "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." Measurement has been corrected for at that point, so the residual can only be attributed to selection or novelty, and the comment shows neither.

- **Selection.** Selection was not corrected for (see point 3 below).
- **Novelty.** Novelty is put forward as a hypothesis, then reasoned about as if it were established. The phrase "burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is rhetoric, not evidence.

The Varden case-processing stratum undercuts the conclusion further. It is randomised, uses administrative output records and timesheet hours, and runs for nine months. It found output per actual hour up **12.5%** (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4). That design removes self-selection, manager rating bias, and the scheduled-hours denominator, which are the comment's three main mechanisms. Varden staff also didn't choose the change, which weakens the novelty story.

The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum finding "the most reliable finding in the literature." It then ignores the case-processing finding from the same trial, which is at least as precise. That is selective citation.

The convergence is the most informative point across all three documents. Correcting Halden's data gives about +11% per actual hour, and Varden's randomised case-processing estimate is +12.5%. Two very different designs land in the same place.

### 2. The novelty argument is untested, although the data to test it exist

The Halden output index was collected **monthly**, and the authors have the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, output should decline from month 3 to month 6, as energy did. The comment never checks this. Instead it extrapolates a straight line through two survey points for a different variable, self-reported energy. That is the weakest argument in the paper, and it is the one the conclusion rests on.

There are other problems with the energy argument:
- Energy rose from 0 to 0.61 and then fell to 0.29. A rise followed by a plateau fits two points just as well as a straight line down to zero.
- Energy is not output. A drop in reported enthusiasm does not mean productivity falls by the same amount.

### 3. The abstract says attrition was corrected, but it wasn't

The abstract states that "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%, and attrition is the first of them. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The nine withdrawers are not in any row.

This could have been addressed with bounds. For example, the authors could assign the withdrawers the lowest observed output, or 80 (equal to the scheduled-hours ratio), and show the effect on the estimate. The correction would probably push the figure down. But its size is unknown, and the abstract implies it has been done.

### 4. Some of the record-based output measures are partly inputs

"Billable hours delivered" counts hours worked, so it falls when hours are cut, whether or not productivity changed. If professional-services firms are among the 23 with records, part of the gap between 98.9 and 95.1 may be mechanical rather than manager optimism. The comment should report the gap separately for organisations whose records are true output counts, such as tickets, units and cases.

### 5. The comment applies standards to Varden that it doesn't meet itself

- **No confidence intervals.** The headline 10.8% rests on 17 non-randomly selected organisations, with no confidence interval or standard error anywhere in the comment.
- **Retail.** The 3-organisation retail figure (−11.2%) is also presented without uncertainty.
- **A double standard on small samples.** The comment dismisses Varden's 7-office correlation as the kind of thing that "does not replicate." Yet its own conclusion leans on a two-point extrapolation of a survey measure.

The data note correctly says the corrected estimates describe subsets, not the whole pilot. The abstract and conclusion then generalise to "reduced-hours schemes" in general, well beyond even the full Halden sample.

### 6. The comment misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis

The comment presents Varden as citing meetings "as a mechanism," and describes the subgroup as "selected for analysis after the results were known." In fact:

- The meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request.
- The Varden authors said explicitly that the correlation "cannot establish a mechanism."
- They registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

The underlying caution is fair. Seven offices and r = 0.71 is weak evidence, and I noted the missing baseline earlier. But the comment is criticising a claim the Varden authors didn't make.

## Synthesis across all three documents

**Well supported:**
- Output per hour measured against scheduled hours overstates the gain by about half. The two independent estimates are 23% → 11% (Halden corrected) and 22% → 12.5% (Varden).
- Actual hours fall by about 13–14%, not 20%.
- Where output depends on staff being present, output per employee falls by roughly 10%, and service suffers.

**Reasonably supported, but short-run only:**
- In backlog-type and knowledge work, output per actual hour rises by about 10–12%.
- Output per employee falls slightly, by about 2–5%.

**Unresolved:**
- Durability. Nine months is the longest evidence available. Varden's 24-month follow-up and a month-by-month analysis of Halden's output index are the obvious tests.
- Cost per unit of output, including overtime pay. Neither study reports it.
- Mechanism: rest, meeting cuts, or effort under observation.

**Not supported by any of the three documents:**
- Halden's claim that the model is sector-general.
- Varga and Holm's claim that the gains are entirely an artifact.

The comment is a valuable correction to Halden. It goes too far when it turns "the gain is smaller than reported and may not last" into "there is no gain."
